title: Listening in record stores; Jack Teagarden changes the trombone
summary: Lester and Phillips listened to new records at the store, including Red Nichols; Phillips credits Teagarden with changing trombone playing and mentions Jimmy Harrison.

bands.name: Red Nichols and His Five Pennies

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: it is now. They didn't have no radio or nothing. But those were the ones that we... See, what we used to do, Les and all of us, we used to go to town and we used to go to the record store, and listen to records. See, because they let you listen to them. They'd give you a bunch of records to play, and tell you the newest ones they had out. We'd listen to, like, "Five Pennies" by Red Nichols...
Red Nichols and his Five Pennies.
No, that's the name of the tune. They had a tune named "Five Pennies." And they had "Play It, Red." "Dinah."
That's a recording by Red Nichols?

Yeah. Jack Teagarden played a hell of a solo on it. He had everybody... See, because Jack Teagarden changed trombone around. See, before he came along, cats was playing slide horn. So they said, "DA-AA-AAT..." But he come along, "BUH-DA-BE/DAH-DA-BE/DA-DAT, BAH-BAH-BAH-BO, BAH-BU-BAH-BO-DA-BU..." -- playing on of them things, playin' riffs. Only it wasn't slide. So he's the one that changed the trombones around. Everybody then was copying him. Like, all trombone players.
Did you ever hear Jimmy Harrison back then?
Yeah. He was on the same kick like Jack Teagarden. But he didn't do enough recording or nothin' like that for people to hear him, and he died early.
